intro: Choose the languages your business genuinely needs and which one is your default. The planner returns a recommended URL structure, the exact hreflang set each of your chosen pages will need, and a translation-quality checklist scoped to the languages you picked — not a generic one. Nothing here is scanned from a real website; every recommendation is built only from the languages and default you select.

languageOptions.name: German
languageOptions.swissVariantNote: Recommended over plain "de" for any business specifically targeting Swiss German-speaking customers, since Swiss High German differs from Germany’s in spelling (ss, not ß) and some vocabulary.

languageOptions.name: French
languageOptions.swissVariantNote: Plain "fr" does not distinguish Swiss French content from France-targeted French content to search engines. Use fr-CH if that distinction matters to your business.

languageOptions.name: Italian
languageOptions.swissVariantNote: Plain "it" does not distinguish Swiss Italian (Ticino) content from Italy-targeted Italian content. Use it-CH if that distinction matters to your business.

languageOptions.name: English
languageOptions.swissVariantNote: English is not a Swiss national language, so no Swiss-specific regional variant applies here; plain "en" is standard.

urlPatternOptions.label: Locale-prefixed subfolders (example.ch/en/, example.ch/it/…)
urlPatternOptions.whenToUse: The right default for nearly every Swiss SME or growing business. One domain accumulates one pool of ranking authority; adding a language later costs a folder, not a migration.
urlPatternOptions.tradeOffs: Requires a routing layer that can serve different content per locale prefix under one domain — standard in any modern CMS or framework, but worth confirming your current platform actually supports it before committing.

urlPatternOptions.label: Subdomains (en.example.ch, it.example.ch…)
urlPatternOptions.whenToUse: Only when hosting infrastructure genuinely differs per market (e.g. a separate application per region for technical reasons unrelated to language).
urlPatternOptions.tradeOffs: Search engines have historically treated subdomains close enough to independent sites that ranking authority does not flow between them as cleanly as within one domain. Rarely worth it just to add a language.

urlPatternOptions.label: Separate country domains (example.ch, example.de, example.it…)
urlPatternOptions.whenToUse: Only at a scale with genuinely separate national entities, separate legal structures and separate marketing budgets per country — not simply "we want to look local."
urlPatternOptions.tradeOffs: Each domain starts its own ranking authority at zero and needs its own backlink profile built up independently. The most expensive option to maintain long-term.

urlPatternOptions.label: Query parameters (example.ch/?lang=en)
urlPatternOptions.whenToUse: Not recommended for a real multilingual SEO strategy under any common scenario.
urlPatternOptions.tradeOffs: Search engines generally treat parameterized variants of one URL as the same page unless painstakingly configured otherwise. This is the pattern most responsible for a "multilingual" site whose second language never actually ranks.

recommendationLogic.description: Given a chosen default locale and a set of additional target locales, the planner always recommends the locale-prefixed subfolder pattern (flagging the other three as generally unsuitable, with their specific reasons shown) and then generates: (1) the URL shape for the default locale (no prefix, at the domain root) and for each additional locale (domain + "/" + locale-code + "/" + a reminder to choose a properly localized slug per language, not a translated copy of the default slug); (2) the exact reciprocal hreflang tag set every one of those pages needs, including itself; (3) the x-default recommendation (point it at the default locale, or at English if English is one of the chosen locales and the business expects international visitors); (4) one canonical reminder: every locale page’s canonical must point at itself, never at the default-locale URL.
recommendationLogic.hreflangRule: For N chosen locales, every one of the N pages must carry N hreflang tags (one per locale, including itself) plus one x-default tag — never fewer, and every tag must be mirrored on every other locale’s page or all of them are ignored.
recommendationLogic.xDefaultRule: x-default → English if English is among the chosen locales; otherwise → the chosen default locale. This is a fallback for visitors whose browser language matches none of your locales, not a ranking mechanism.
recommendationLogic.canonicalRule: Every locale’s page canonical → its own URL. Never canonicalize a translated page back to the default-locale version — doing so tells search engines to treat it as a copy, not an original.

translationQualityChecklist.item: Launch copy for every chosen language was written or reviewed by a person fluent in that language and familiar with the target reader — not shipped as an unedited machine-translation pass.
translationQualityChecklist.whyItMatters: A grammatically correct translation can still answer the wrong underlying question if it keeps the source language’s structure, order and idioms instead of being rewritten for the reader actually asking in that language.

translationQualityChecklist.item: Each language version was checked for whether local searchers actually ask the same underlying question, not just the same question in different words.
translationQualityChecklist.whyItMatters: A German-speaking searcher and an English-speaking searcher researching the same service often have a different starting assumption or concern — translating words without adjusting framing answers the wrong version of the question.

translationQualityChecklist.item: Business idioms and figures of speech were rewritten for meaning in each language, not translated literally.
translationQualityChecklist.whyItMatters: A phrase that is a natural idiom in the source language (e.g. a German business phrase meaning "one team handles it all") often becomes nonsensical or flat when translated word for word.

translationQualityChecklist.item: Each language has its own distinct, properly localized URL slug — not the default-locale slug with a language-code prefix stapled in front.
translationQualityChecklist.whyItMatters: A slug is content too. A slug that is just the default-locale word with a prefix added misses a real opportunity to match how speakers of that language actually search, and looks unmistakably like an afterthought.

translationQualityChecklist.item: A deliberate decision was made about whether to use a plain language code or a Swiss-specific regional code (de-CH, fr-CH, it-CH) for each language, based on whether distinguishing Swiss content from Germany/France/Italy content actually matters to the business.
translationQualityChecklist.whyItMatters: A plain "fr" or "it" hreflang code does not tell search engines your French or Italian content is Swiss-specific rather than France- or Italy-targeted — only the regional variant does that.

translationQualityChecklist.item: Someone is named and responsible for keeping every published language current — not just for launching it once.
translationQualityChecklist.whyItMatters: A translated page that stops being updated while the default-locale version keeps changing becomes a visible, dated mismatch that damages trust more than not having that language at all.

translationQualityChecklist.item: The site does not create hreflang links, canonical claims or language-switcher links to a translation that has not actually been written yet.
translationQualityChecklist.whyItMatters: A language switcher or hreflang tag that implies a page exists in a language it does not is a broken promise the moment a visitor or a search engine checks it.

errorStates.noLocalesSelected: If a reader has selected zero target locales beyond the default, show a neutral prompt: "Select at least one additional language to see a recommended structure" — do not show an empty or misleading recommendation.
errorStates.defaultNotSelected: If no default locale is chosen, default the planner’s own selection to nothing and prompt for it first — the URL shape and x-default logic both depend on knowing which locale is the default.
errorStates.sameLocaleTwice: If a reader somehow selects the same locale as both default and target, ignore the duplicate silently rather than showing it twice in the output.

outputSections.label: Recommended URL structure
outputSections.description: The exact URL shape for the default locale and for every additional chosen locale, using the subfolder pattern, with a one-line reason the other three patterns were not recommended.

outputSections.label: hreflang plan
outputSections.description: The exact reciprocal hreflang tag set every chosen locale’s page needs to carry, plus the recommended x-default target, written out as ready-to-check tag lines, not just described in prose.

outputSections.label: Canonical rule
outputSections.description: A one-line, locale-specific reminder that every page’s canonical points at itself, never at the default-locale version.

outputSections.label: Translation-quality checklist
outputSections.description: The seven-item checklist above, shown for every chosen locale beyond the default, each item togglable as done/not done — no scoring, just a working list.

disclaimer: This planner generates a URL, hreflang and canonical starting point from the languages you select — it does not scan, crawl or audit any real website, and it does not guarantee a specific search ranking or AI-citation outcome for any language. It is a structural starting point for a conversation with whoever builds or maintains your site, not a technical SEO audit or a legal or accessibility certification. All logic runs in your browser; nothing you select is transmitted or stored.
